subject: Capacity hedge & demand-smoothing: committed slab vs transient burst for Helio Systems
messages:
From: Soojin Lee <soojin_lee@redwood.ai>
To: Alicia Park <apark@helio-systems.com>, Marcus Chen <mchen@helio-systems.com>
Cc: Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.ai>, Vanessa Ortiz <vanessa_ortiz@redwood.ai>
Date: Tue, 14 Sep 2026 08:23:00 -0700
Subject: Capacity hedge & demand-smoothing: committed slab vs transient burst for Helio Systems

Hi Alicia / Marcus —

Thanks again for the time yesterday. Attached is a concise capacity matrix and a first-pass autoscale policy that maps to the two contract options we discussed: (A) committed slab with headroom credits, and (B) smaller committed node pool + higher transient burst allowance.

Key assumptions in the matrix (high-level):
- Baseline steady RPS: 120 requests/s (90th pct usage across day)
- Peak short spikes up to 480 requests/s (10–15 minute windows, ~3x baseline)
- Typical sequence length and token mix: mixes of short chat + 5–10% long-form generation

Trade-offs we highlighted:
- Committed slab gives deterministic latency and lower unit cost during sustained loads, but requires a larger committed invoice and a 30–60 day ramp to scale up further.
- Transient burst (ephemeral) is flexible and cheaper initially, but can incur cold starts and pre-warm needs for predictable tail latency; we account for pre-warm lanes in the policy.

Attached: capacity_matrix_v2.xlsx (walks through sizing by node type), autoscale_policy_draft.pdf (cooldowns, pre-warm thresholds, eviction priorities), and a draft SLA clause for burst guarantees.

Ask: please review the matrix and the two commercial options. If you lean toward Option A (slab + headroom), we’ll provide a committed sizing annex and an estimated ramp schedule. If Option B, we’ll map burst cost assumptions to your monthly forecast and propose a smaller committed minimum.

Next steps I recommend:
1) Confirm target 90th/95th pct SLOs for tail latency we should design to.
2) Tell us the acceptable blackout window for burst evictions (e.g., tolerate best-effort eviction vs require guaranteed pre-warm).
3) If procurement is involved, loop them in and we can produce a single-page commitment matrix for signature.

Happy to hop on a quick call tomorrow to walk through the matrix live.

Thanks,
Soojin
Soojin Lee
Account Lead, Redwood Inference

Date: Wed, 15 Sep 2026 09:04:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Capacity hedge & demand-smoothing: committed slab vs transient burst for Helio Systems

Thanks Soojin — this is helpful. A few clarifying questions from our side before procurement jumps in: 

1) Cold starts: you call out pre-warm lanes — can you quantify expected tail latency delta (p95, p99) for ephemeral bursts vs pre-warmed slab? We need numbers for our SRE team.
2) Billing model: for transient burst, is billing per GPU-minute or per-token equivalent? Also, how do headroom credits get applied when both slab and transient are in play?
3) Eviction behavior: in the worst case when capacity is constrained, what's Redwood's fallback? Will requests be queued, rate-limited, or routed to a lower-spec model? We need a clear degradation path for our product team.

Marcus and I are leaning toward a hybrid: a modest committed slab for baseline + defined burst pool for marketing spikes. Procurement wants a simple one-page that shows expected monthly cost bands — that would help speed approvals.

Can Karthik / Vanessa and Soojin provide the latency deltas and the billing examples? If we can get that in the next 48 hours, procurement can do an initial approval.

— Alicia
Alicia Park
Head of Platform, Helio Systems
From: Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.ai>
To: Alicia Park <apark@helio-systems.com>, Marcus Chen <mchen@helio-systems.com>
Cc: Soojin Lee <soojin_lee@redwood.ai>, Vanessa Ortiz <vanessa_ortiz@redwood.ai>
Date: Wed, 15 Sep 2026 11:12:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Capacity hedge & demand-smoothing: committed slab vs transient burst for Helio Systems

Alicia — quick answers and an example cost table below. Will follow with a short call if helpful.

Latency delta (typical):
- Pre-warmed committed slab (p95/p99): 120ms / 250ms
- Transient burst with pre-warm lane (allocated warm GPUs): 150ms / 320ms
- Cold-start ephemeral instance (no pre-warm): 350ms / 900ms (depends on model size and quant state)

Billing model:
- Committed slab: invoiced as monthly reserved GPU-hours at discounted rate (per-GPU-hour).
- Transient burst: billed per-usage (per-GPU-minute) + per-token generation at hosted rates when applicable.
- Headroom credits: applied as a monthly offset to transient consumption charges until credits are exhausted. Credits do not reduce committed slab invoice.

Degradation path when capacity constrained:
1) Automated routing attempts: route to regional spare capacity (cross-region fallback if enabled).
2) If no spare capacity, automatic graceful fallback to smaller model variant (we list compatible variants in the SLA) — this preserves availability but may reduce output quality.
3) As last resort, rate-limited responses with clear 429 and Retry-After headers.

Example cost bands (illustrative):
- Option A (Large committed slab: 20 GPUs c7x-large): baseline monthly invoice $60,000; expected transient overage (worst-month spikes) $5–10k after headroom credits.
- Option B (Small committed slab: 8 GPUs + transient buffer): baseline monthly invoice $26,000; expected transient consumption $12–25k depending on spike volume.

Notes: the numbers above assume your long-form generation is capped to the token mix we discussed. We can tighten the forecast with your historical RPS/peak cadence if you can share a 30-day sample.

Proposed next steps:
- Soojin: can you push the revised one-page commitment matrix (A vs B, with the numeric bands and latency rows) to the shared Drive? 
- Vanessa: can you confirm pre-warm lane sizing and cooldown windows we recommend for Helio’s usage pattern? I suggest a 5-minute burst pre-warm window with a 3-minute cooldown for aggressive workloads.

I can join procurement call Friday if useful.

Thanks,
Karthik
Head, Solutions — Redwood Inference
From: Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.ai>

Date: Thu, 16 Sep 2026 16:05:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Capacity hedge & demand-smoothing: committed slab vs transient burst for Helio Systems

Alicia / Marcus — looping in a succinct commercial proposal and a path to close. Good summaries from Soojin and Karthik. A few clarifications and a proposed sign-off runbook: 

Commercial clarification:
- We will publish a one-page appendix with the chosen option (A or B) that lists committed GPUs, headroom credits, burst upper-limit, and billing cadence. That appendix becomes part of the MSA.
- If you choose Option B and you exceed agreed burst thresholds for three consecutive months, we’ll auto-trigger a sizing review to recommend additional committed capacity (no automatic invoice changes without sign-off).

Operational sign-off runbook (to keep production safe during spikes):
1) Pre-warm lanes: Redwood will reserve up to X GPUs for 3–10 minutes when pre-warm thresholds are met (we’ll set X based on the committed choice).
2) Cooldown & eviction: 3-minute cooldown by default; ephemeral instances are evicted LRU across non-prod tags.
3) Fallback and notification: on degradation, Redwood will notify Helio SRE and throttle new sessions; we’ll also open a high-priority ops ticket to discuss mitigation.

Action items to close this week: 
- Soojin: update the capacity matrix with cost bands tied to Option A and Option B and add an explicit pre-warm sizing row. (Due: EOD Friday)
- Alicia / Marcus: confirm which option procurement prefers and share 30-day RPS sample if possible.
- Procurement (Helio): if the one-pager is acceptable, sign the appendix and we’ll attach to the MSA.

If it helps, I can prepare a redlined appendix for Option A that matches the SLA targets Karthik listed. Otherwise, let's book 30 minutes Friday to finalize.

Best,
Ben Carter
VP, Sales — Redwood Inference
